lesson.title: When Higher Is Better: The Maximum Value of a Parabola
lesson.summary: When a parabola opens downward, its vertex sits higher than every other point on the curve, and the vertex's y-coordinate is called the function's maximum value.
lesson.body:
You saw in the vertex section that whether the vertex is the lowest or highest point on a parabola depends on the sign of a. When a is negative, the parabola opens downward, and the vertex becomes the single highest point the graph ever reaches. The y-coordinate of that vertex is called the maximum value of the function: no input produces a larger output than that.

This shows up constantly in real situations that rise and then fall, exactly the kind of pattern a straight line could never model. Consider a ball thrown upward, whose height in meters t seconds after being thrown is modeled by h(t) = -t^2 + 4t + 5. Here a = -1, which is negative, so the parabola opens downward and a maximum height does exist.

Find it the same way you find any vertex: x = -b/(2a), using t in place of x here since the input represents time. With a = -1 and b = 4, t = -4/(2·(-1)) = -4/(-2) = 2. Substitute t = 2 back into h(t) to get the maximum height: h(2) = -(2)^2 + 4(2) + 5 = -4 + 8 + 5 = 9. So the ball reaches a maximum height of 9 meters, at 2 seconds after being thrown.

It is worth double-checking that this really is the highest point by testing values on either side. At t = 1, h(1) = -1 + 4 + 5 = 8. At t = 3, h(3) = -9 + 12 + 5 = 8. Both are less than 9, and both are the same, 1 second on either side of t = 2, which is exactly what you would expect from the axis of symmetry at t = 2. Everywhere else on the curve gives a smaller height, confirming that 9 meters really is the maximum, not just a value picked out by the formula.
